opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that Ethernet has never really stood still. People sometimes think of it as this old, fixed technology, but what "Ethernet" means today is almost nothing like what it meant in the 1980s. It's survived because it keeps reinventing itself while keeping the parts that matter: a huge ecosystem, many vendors competing, and enormous economies of scale. When you're building networks at the scale we need for AI training, with tens or hundreds of thousands of GPUs, that ecosystem really matters. You want switch silicon on a fast cadence, optics getting cheaper and faster, and you don't want to be locked into a single supplier.

The other part is that the bits that historically made Ethernet look weaker for high-performance computing weren't really about the link layer. They were about the transport protocols and how congestion and loss get handled. Traditional RoCE, for example, assumed a lossless network and was very sensitive to packet ordering, so you ended up with fragile configurations. Flow control could cause head-of-line blocking, and things got hard to debug at scale.

What we've learned, and a lot of the work around things like Ultra Ethernet reflects this, is that you can fix those problems at the endpoints. If the NIC can spray packets across many paths, tolerate reordering, recover quickly from loss, and respond to congestion signals intelligently, then you don't need the network itself to be perfect. You can use all the paths in a big multi-plane fabric at once, route around failures in microseconds rather than seconds, and keep utilization high even with very bursty collective traffic.

So for me, Ethernet is a foundation not because it's magic, but because it gives you a cheap, fast, widely available substrate, and then you put the intelligence where it can evolve fastest. That combination is what scales, and I think it'll keep scaling as these clusters keep growing.

r001.rationale: It says Ethernet benefits from a huge ecosystem, competing vendors, and economies of scale, with faster, cheaper switches and optics.

r002.rationale: It explains that NICs at the endpoints can handle reordering, loss recovery, and congestion, letting the network itself be less perfect while the Ethernet substrate scales.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that Ethernet has already been through this movie several times. Every decade or so, somebody declares that Ethernet can't keep up with whatever the hot workload is, and every time the ecosystem catches up and then overtakes the proprietary alternative, because the economics are just overwhelming. The volume of Ethernet silicon that gets built, the number of vendors competing on optics and switches, the depth of the engineering talent that knows how to operate it at scale – nothing else comes close. So when we're building out networks for AI clusters that are going to run for years and keep growing, betting on the thing with the broadest ecosystem is the sensible long-term call.

The second point is that the actual physical link technology is the same. Whether you call it InfiniBand or Ethernet, you're pushing the same SerDes, the same optics, the same bandwidth generations. The differences live higher up – in how you do congestion control, how you do load balancing across paths, how you handle loss. And those are things we can engineer. That's really where the interesting work is.

The weaknesses of classic Ethernet for this workload are well known. The traffic patterns in training are very bursty and highly synchronised – everyone talks to everyone at the same moment during a collective – and the default behaviour of flow hashing onto a single path and dropping packets when you get a hotspot is pretty bad for that. But none of those are intrinsic to Ethernet. You can spray packets across all the available paths instead of pinning a flow to one. You can do congestion control that reacts in a round-trip time rather than waiting for queues to build up. You can handle the reordering in the NIC so the application doesn't see it. Once you do those things, you get the tail latency behaviour you need, and the collective finishes when the slowest flow finishes, so tail latency is really what matters.

And then there's scale. These clusters are getting enormous. At some point you need a fabric that can span a whole building, or multiple buildings, with tens or hundreds of thousands of endpoints, and you want the same operational tooling, the same telemetry, the same people running it that run the rest of your infrastructure. Ethernet lets us do that. We don't have to maintain a separate island with its own skills and its own supply chain.

So I'd put it this way: Ethernet isn't the foundation because it's perfect out of the box. It's the foundation because it's the substrate that the whole industry is investing in, the raw bandwidth roadmap is as good as anything else, and the problems it does have are solvable in the transport layer – which is exactly where we've been doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says Ethernet benefits from a broad ecosystem of silicon, vendors, and engineering talent, and that the industry is investing in its roadmap.

r002.rationale: It mentions handling packet reordering in the NIC and engineering transport features, but does not explain that putting intelligence at the edge lets network cores scale as Ethernet scales.

astra-6.text:
I think the key thing about Ethernet is that it keeps evolving. It’s not one fixed technology with one fixed speed. There’s a very broad industry investing in making it faster, cheaper, and more power efficient, and that gives us a foundation we can keep building on as these systems grow.

But Ethernet by itself isn’t the whole answer. An AI supercomputer has a very demanding traffic pattern: lots of machines communicating at once, and the computation can end up waiting for whichever transfer finishes last. So you have to design the network as a system—the topology, the congestion control, and the way traffic is spread across the available paths.

The attraction is that we can innovate in those areas while benefiting from the Ethernet ecosystem underneath. We don’t have to reinvent every component to build a network that’s suited to AI.

r001.rationale: The response says Ethernet benefits from broad industry investment and describes innovating in network design while using the Ethernet ecosystem underneath.

r002.rationale: It discusses topology, congestion control, and traffic distribution, but does not say that network intelligence at the edge lets network cores scale with Ethernet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing about Ethernet is that it’s an ecosystem, not just a particular link speed. You have lots of companies investing in switches, optics, network interfaces, and the software around them. That gives you a very broad base of innovation to build on as the networks get larger and faster.

Now, connecting everything with Ethernet doesn’t by itself give you a good AI supercomputer network. These workloads are very demanding: lots of machines communicating at once, and the whole computation can end up waiting for the slowest transfer. So you have to get congestion control, load balancing, and reliability right.

But those are things we can evolve while building on that Ethernet foundation. We don’t have to reinvent every component of the network each time we scale up, and that’s a very powerful place to start.

r001.rationale: The response says Ethernet provides a broad ecosystem of companies investing in switches, optics, interfaces, and software, creating a broad base of innovation for larger and faster networks.

r002.rationale: The response discusses evolving congestion control, load balancing, and reliability, but does not say that placing network intelligence at the edge lets network cores scale with Ethernet.
